title: Interfaces vs Abstract Classes: Quick Revision
summary: Quick revision notes on contracts versus partial implementations, multiple interface implementation, default methods, choosing between them, programming to an interface, and the template method pattern, with Java and Python examples.

chapters.title: Contracts vs Partial Implementations
points: Interface = pure contract: declares what a type can do (method signatures) with no state; Java `interface Shape { double area(); }`
Abstract class = partial implementation: shared state and concrete methods plus abstract methods subclasses must fill in
Python has no interface keyword: use `abc.ABC` with `@abstractmethod`, or `typing.Protocol` for structural (duck-typed) contracts
Abstract classes and interfaces cannot be instantiated; Python raises TypeError when abstract methods are unimplemented, Java fails at compile time
Mental model: interface = 'can do' (capability), abstract class = 'is a' (shared base with common code)

chapters.title: Multiple Interface Implementation
points: Java: a class extends one class but implements many interfaces: `class Duck implements Flyer, Swimmer`
Python: multiple inheritance from several ABCs or Protocols: `class Duck(Flyer, Swimmer)`; MRO (C3 linearization) decides method lookup order
Diamond problem: two interfaces with the same default method force Java to require an explicit override; resolve with `Flyer.super.move()`
Python resolves diamonds via MRO and `super()`; check order with `Duck.__mro__`
Java forbids multiple inheritance of state, so only one abstract class can be extended; this is why interfaces carry multiple capabilities

chapters.title: Default Methods and Choosing Between Them
points: Java 8 `default` methods give interfaces a body so new methods can be added without breaking existing implementers: `default void log() {...}`
Interface default methods cannot hold instance fields; they can only call other interface methods
Python equivalent: ABCs can include concrete methods; Protocols can define default bodies that explicit subclasses inherit
Choose interface when unrelated classes share a capability, you need multiple inheritance, or you want a minimal contract
Choose abstract class when subclasses share state or constructor logic, need non-public members, or you want to control a common skeleton

chapters.title: Programming to an Interface
points: Depend on the abstraction, not the concrete class: `List<String> xs = new ArrayList<>();` and `def run(store: Storage)`
Callers accept the interface type in parameters, fields and return types, so implementations can be swapped without touching callers
Enables dependency injection and testing: pass a fake `InMemoryRepo` instead of a real `DbRepo` in unit tests
Python example: `class Repo(Protocol): def get(self, id: int) -> User: ...` and any class with `get` satisfies it
Mistake: creating an interface for every class with a single implementation and no variation; add one when you need a seam

chapters.title: Abstract Classes and the Template Method
points: Template method: the base class defines the algorithm skeleton in a concrete method, and subclasses override the varying steps
Java: `abstract class Report { final void generate() { load(); format(); save(); } abstract void format(); }`; `final` prevents overriding the skeleton
Python: `class Report(ABC): def generate(self): self.load(); self.format(); self.save()` with `@abstractmethod def format(self)`
Hook methods are optional steps with an empty or default body that subclasses may override, for example `beforeSave()`
Mistake: calling an overridable method from a constructor, because the subclass fields are not initialised yet; and Python has no `final`, so document it or use `typing.final`

chapters.title: Interfaces vs Abstract Classes Cheat Sheet
points: Interface: capability, no state, many per class, default methods for evolution; abstract class: shared state and code, one per class
Java syntax: `interface X { void a(); default void b() {} }` and `abstract class Y { abstract void a(); void b() {} }`
Python syntax: `class X(ABC): @abstractmethod def a(self): ...` and `class P(Protocol): def a(self) -> None: ...`
Decision rule: start with an interface, add an abstract class to share code, and combine both with an abstract skeleton implementing the interface
Interview: expect questions on diamond resolution, why interfaces cannot hold state, template method vs strategy, and Protocol vs ABC
